fact_notes: Automatic shut-off fuel nozzles are purely mechanical: no electronic sensor or power in the nozzle (HowStuffWorks 'How Does a Gas Pump Know When to Stop?'; Hagerty 'How the Venturi effect enables gas pump shutoffs').
Near the tip of the spout there is a small sensing hole connected by a thin tube back to a chamber in the nozzle body.
Fuel flowing through a venturi in the nozzle creates low pressure that draws air in through the sensing hole and tube while the hole is uncovered.
When fuel rises and covers the hole, air can no longer enter; suction builds in the chamber, pulls a diaphragm, which releases a latch/linkage so the spring-loaded valve snaps shut (the click).
Foam or splash-back covering the hole (or a poorly inserted nozzle) triggers the same mechanism early - the familiar premature click.
